analysis.one_liner: Bans possession and transfer of handguns not deemed suitable for sporting purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal gun law to make it illegal for anyone to possess or transfer a handgun that the Treasury Secretary has not determined is suitable for sporting purposes. Guns people already lawfully owned could be kept, but they could never be sold, given away, or inherited, since transfers would be banned outright. Because most handguns sold in America are general-purpose self-defense or target guns rather than formally designated sporting guns, this would amount to a federal near-ban on the civilian handgun market going forward.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, communities affected by handgun violence would benefit from a dramatically smaller supply of handguns, since nearly all new sales and transfers of non-sporting handguns would become federal crimes [S2] [S3]. Gun violence-prevention advocates would gain the strongest federal handgun restriction ever enacted. Gun owners who already legally possessed handguns could keep them, though they could not sell or give them away [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to possess or transfer any non-sporting handgun that has moved in interstate or foreign commerce, with penalties under the federal firearms statute [S2] [S3].
Grandfathers only the continuous, otherwise lawful possession of handguns people already owned, so existing owners would not face prosecution for the guns in their hands [S2] [S3].
Defines 'sporting handgun' using the same criteria the Treasury Secretary applies to import determinations, meaning ordinary self-defense handguns would generally fall under the ban [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners would bear the largest cost: they could keep existing handguns but could never transfer them to anyone, so no sales, gifts, or inheritance of even grandfathered guns [S3]. The firearms industry would lose virtually the entire civilian handgun market, since new non-sporting handguns could not lawfully be sold or transferred at all [S2] [S3]. People who want a handgun for self-defense in the future would have no legal way to acquire one.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers transfers even of grandfathered guns, meaning law-abiding owners could not sell, gift, or pass down handguns they legally possess, an effective slow elimination of private handgun ownership without compensation [S3].

The sporting-purposes test is decided by a federal agency, so nearly all common self-defense and target handguns would be banned by administrative determination rather than by explicit congressional listing of which guns are prohibited [S3].

The bill does nothing to address the millions of handguns already in circulation beyond freezing their transfer, and critics argue a supply-side ban would leave criminals armed while disarming lawful buyers; the bill contains no answer to that objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is an extremely ambitious bill with a genuine trade-off at its center. On one side, a federal ban on nearly all civilian handgun sales and transfers would, over time, greatly shrink the number of handguns in private hands, which supporters argue would reduce handgun deaths. On the other, the costs fall directly on tens of millions of law-abiding gun owners, who could keep their current guns but could never sell, give away, or bequeath them, and on anyone who wants a handgun for self-defense in the future. The bill would have reshaped American life on the most contested gun question there is, and it was introduced with no realistic path to passage: it never received a hearing, let alone a vote, in a Congress controlled by a party opposed to handgun restrictions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to its Crime Subcommittee on January 28, 1997, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on January 21, 1997, with 18 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S3] [S5].
A week later it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, the usual path for firearms bills, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill attracted 64 cosponsors, 63 Democrats and 1 Republican, but never advanced past the subcommittee, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and the firearms industry are better off because the bill died: no federal restriction on handgun possession or transfer was ever enacted. Opponents of handgun bans avoided the most sweeping federal handgun restriction ever proposed without ever having to vote on it.

for.name: Rep. Luis V. Gutierrez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban possession and transfer of non-sporting handguns and recruited 18 original cosponsors [S3] [S5].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Henry Hyde (R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it during the two-year Congress [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 28, 1997, and held no hearing or markup on it; the bill sat there until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 64 cosponsors were Democrats except one Republican, and the bill sat in committee in a House run by Republicans with no action ever scheduled, so support was overwhelmingly Democratic and the block was procedural rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated nearly the entire civilian handgun market, since non-sporting handguns could not lawfully be sold, transferred, or even possessed going forward [S2] [S3]. Its interest ran against gun-control supporters but alongside the many ordinary gun owners who would have lost the ability to buy, sell, or inherit handguns.

Owners of handguns acquired before the effective date could keep them, but any transfer, including sale, gift, or inheritance, would be a federal crime [S3]. They keep their guns but lose every right over them except personal possession.
